# Diagnosing Hesitation and Rough Shifting on a 1999 Subaru Forester

A 1999 Subaru Forester exhibiting poor acceleration, hesitation during takeoff, and rough shifting at speed presents a classic fuel/air mixture problem rather than a simple ignition or transmission issue. The specific symptom of the engine bogging down when you press harder on the gas pedalâonly to recover when backing offâis the diagnostic key here. This behavior indicates that the Engine Control Unit (ECU) is struggling to maintain stability under load, causing it to momentarily cut fuel or advance timing incorrectly before retreating to a "sweet spot" in the throttle map.

The data you provided from your Snap-On scan tool offers a definitive starting point for troubleshooting. You are observing Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) values between 22% and 37% at idle and cruise, with Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT) sitting between 25% and 30%. These numbers are critically high. A positive fuel trim indicates the ECU is constantly adding fuel because it detects a vacuum leak or insufficient fuel delivery. When you floor the pedal, the STFT drops to -10% and LTFT to -5%, which suggests the ECU is momentarily cutting fuel to prevent flooding or over-fueling as it tries to stabilize the mixture.

Before you proceed to pull injectorsâa labor-intensive process that often yields diminishing returns on a vehicle of this ageâyou must address the root cause of the lean condition. The fact that you replaced the throttle body and gasket, yet the issue persists, suggests the problem is not located at the intake air path immediately upstream of the throttle plate. While a clogged throttle body can cause issues, the persistent high trim values imply an unaccounted source of unmetered air entering the system after the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor or a restriction in the fuel delivery system itself.

The O2 code you mentioned is a significant clue. Even if it has been stored for years without affecting drivability, the underlying condition that triggered it likely remains unresolved. An oxygen sensor reading out of its normal range will cause the ECU to swing trims aggressively. If the sensor is failing or contaminated by oil fouling (common in older Subaru EJ25 engines), the feedback loop becomes erratic, leading to the hesitation you experience.

Regarding fuel pressure, 28 to 33 psi is generally within the acceptable range for a Forester with an E-47 fuel pump, provided the regulator diaphragm hasn't failed internally. However, high trim values often point to a restriction in the fuel filter or a collapsing hose under load that isn't apparent at static pressure. Since you have already installed a new fuel filter, check the return line and the fuel pump screen for debris that could restrict flow during wide-open throttle (WOT) acceleration.

If the air/fuel mixture is confirmed to be lean despite high fuel pressure, inspect the intake manifold gaskets. On the 1999 model year, these rubber gaskets can shrink over time, creating small vacuum leaks that the MAF sensor cannot compensate for at higher RPMs. The "sweet spot" behavior you described is typical of an engine hunting for a stable mixture point as it attempts to correct a lean condition dynamically.

Addressing the hesitation requires isolating the source of the unmetered air or the fuel restriction. Cleaning the injectors with a chemical flush is a logical next step before disassembly, though replacing them is rarely necessary unless they are mechanically stuck. If vacuum leaks are ruled out and fuel delivery is confirmed sufficient via a flow test, the issue may lie within the ECU's adaptation logic due to a failing oxygen sensor or a faulty MAF sensor that is under-reporting airflow.
